questions.stem: You are examining Kathy, 78, in the GP clinic for worsening breathlessness with orthopnoea. You position her and find a venous pulsation in the right side of her neck. The examiner asks how you will measure her jugular venous pressure. Which method is correct?
options: Vertical height of the top of the pulsation above the clavicle, sitting at 90°
Vertical height of the top of the pulsation above the sternal angle, reclined at 45°
Distance along the neck from the sternal angle to the top of the pulsation, at 45°
Vertical height of the top of the pulsation above the sternal angle, lying flat at 0°
questions.why: The JVP is the vertical height in cm from the sternal angle to the top of the internal jugular pulsation, with the patient reclined at 45° and her head turned slightly to the left. The sternal angle sits about 5 cm above the right atrium, and a normal JVP is 3 cm or less. Kathy's is +5 cm.
notes: The clavicle is not the reference point, and sitting at 90° can hide a moderately raised JVP behind the jaw or clavicle.
The JVP is a vertical height, because it measures a column of blood. A distance measured along the slope of the neck overestimates it.
Lying flat, the neck veins fill up to the jaw even in healthy people, so the top of the column can't be seen and the reading is meaningless.

questions.stem: Kathy, 78, has probable new decompensated heart failure with alveolar oedema on X-ray. While you wait in the GP treatment room for the ambulance, she is alert and talking in sentences. Her RR is 22, SpO2 94% on room air and BP 154/86. She has no history of COPD or hypercapnia. What is the most appropriate approach to oxygen and positioning?
options: Sit her upright and give oxygen only if SpO2 falls below 92%, targeting 92 to 96%
Sit her upright and give 15 L/min oxygen via a non-rebreather mask to keep SpO2 at 100%
Lie her flat with legs raised and give 2 L/min oxygen via nasal prongs
Give 2 L/min oxygen via nasal prongs, titrated to an SpO2 of 88 to 92%
questions.why: Australian (TSANZ) guidance is to give oxygen only when SpO2 is below 92% and to target 92 to 96% in patients without hypercapnic risk. Sitting upright reduces venous return and eases her breathing. Hyperoxia gives no benefit and may cause harm, for example coronary vasoconstriction.
notes: High-flow oxygen aimed at 100% causes hyperoxia without benefit and is not recommended when her saturation is already in the target range.
Lying her flat and raising her legs increases venous return and pulmonary congestion, which makes her orthopnoea worse.
The 88 to 92% target is for patients at risk of hypercapnia, such as those with COPD. Kathy has a 10 pack-year history and no COPD, so her target is 92 to 96%.

questions.stem: Kathy, 78, with suspected heart failure after an NSTEMI, now sleeps propped on 3 pillows. She says the breathlessness comes on within minutes of lying flat and eases when she sits up. Which mechanism best explains her orthopnoea?
options: Lying flat lets abdominal contents splint the diaphragm, reducing vital capacity
Lying flat lowers sympathetic drive, so the failing ventricle contracts less strongly
Lying flat causes bronchial wall oedema and bronchospasm, raising airway resistance
Lying flat shifts blood from legs and gut to the chest, raising LV filling pressure
questions.why: Lying flat sends pooled blood from the legs and gut back to the heart, so venous return rises. The failing left ventricle cannot cope with the extra preload, so pulmonary venous and capillary pressure rise and fluid moves into the lungs within minutes.
notes: Diaphragm splinting matters in obesity, ascites or diaphragm weakness. She has none of these, and in heart failure it plays only a minor part.
Less adrenergic support during sleep is one proposed contributor to PND, which builds over hours. It does not explain breathlessness within minutes of lying down.
Bronchial wall oedema ('cardiac asthma') is a result of pulmonary congestion and is seen with PND. It is not what triggers her breathlessness when she lies flat, and she has no wheeze.

questions.stem: You assess Kathy's JVP on the right side of her neck to estimate her right atrial pressure. She is 78 and has suspected congestive heart failure, and her JVP is +5 cm with a positive hepatojugular reflux. Why is the right internal jugular vein the preferred vein for this assessment?
options: It lies superficial to sternocleidomastoid, so its column is directly visible
It drains through the left brachiocephalic vein, which lengthens the column
It has a valve at its termination that amplifies the a and v waves
It runs in a nearly straight line through the SVC into the right atrium
questions.why: The right IJV runs in an almost straight line via the right brachiocephalic vein and the SVC into the right atrium, so its pulsation reflects right atrial pressure faithfully. It lies deep to sternocleidomastoid, so you usually see its pulsation transmitted through the muscle rather than the vein itself.
notes: The internal jugular vein lies deep to sternocleidomastoid, between its two heads low in the neck. The external jugular vein is the superficial one.
The right IJV joins the right subclavian vein to form the right brachiocephalic vein. A longer, more angled course through the left side would reflect atrial pressure less accurately.
Venous valves do not amplify the waveform. A competent valve would block transmission of pressure, which is one reason the external jugular vein is less reliable.
